title: Momentum (HT only)
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Momentum (HT only) — AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification, section 4.5.7.
meta_desc: GCSE Physics (AQA) practice covering Momentum (HT only), specification section 4.5.7.
final_note: You worked through Momentum (HT only) — 18 specification statements.

concepts.def: A property of a moving object. The specification defines momentum by an equation: momentum is the object's mass multiplied by its velocity. Because velocity appears in the definition, an object has momentum only while it is moving — a stationary object has zero momentum however large its mass is.

The word equation that defines momentum. In the AQA list of equations this is one that students are required to recall, so it must be learned rather than looked up. Both quantities on the right must be in SI units before it is used: mass in kilograms and velocity in metres per second.

The symbol form of the momentum equation: p is momentum, m is mass and v is velocity. It rearranges to m = p / v and to v = p / m, so any one of the three quantities can be found when the other two are known.

Momentum, p, in kilograms metre per second, kg m/s. The unit follows directly from the equation: kilograms (mass) multiplied by metres per second (velocity). It is not the newton, which is the unit of force, and not the joule, which is the unit of energy.

Mass, m, in kilograms, kg. A mass given in grams must be converted to kilograms before p = m v is used — divide by 1000. A value in newtons is a weight, not a mass, and cannot be substituted into the equation.
Velocity, v, in metres per second, m/s. Velocity is the speed of the object in a given direction, so the number substituted into p = m v carries a direction with it.

Because momentum is mass multiplied by velocity, and velocity has a direction, momentum has a direction too. For objects moving along one line, choose one direction as positive; anything moving the other way then has a negative velocity and so a negative momentum. Two objects of equal mass moving towards each other at the same speed have momenta that cancel to zero.

A system that nothing enters and nothing leaves, and on which no external force acts. Conservation of momentum is stated by the specification for a closed system, so the two colliding trolleys, or the two skaters, must be considered together and treated as free from outside forces such as a push from a hand.

The momenta of all the objects in the system added together, with direction taken into account. An object moving in the negative direction contributes a negative amount, so the total can be smaller than either individual momentum, and can be zero.

In a closed system, the total momentum before an event is equal to the total momentum after the event. This is called conservation of momentum. It is what makes an unknown velocity after a collision findable: total momentum after must equal the total worked out before.

concepts.term: Momentum as a model for an event
concepts.def: An event is anything that changes how the objects in a system are moving — most often a collision. Momentum is used as a model for such an event: individual objects gain or lose momentum, but the total for the closed system does not change, so any momentum one object loses has been transferred to the other.

concepts.term: Collision in which the objects join
concepts.def: When two objects collide and move off together, they afterwards have one combined mass and one shared velocity. Total momentum before is worked out from the separate objects; total momentum after is the combined mass multiplied by that shared velocity, and the two totals are equal.

If two objects are stationary and then push each other apart, the total momentum before the event is zero, so the total afterwards must also be zero. The two objects therefore move in opposite directions with momenta of equal size — which means the lighter object moves off with the greater speed.

When a force acts on an object that is moving, or able to move, a change in momentum occurs. The change is written m ∆v, where ∆v is the change in velocity — the final velocity minus the initial velocity — not the final velocity itself. A car of mass 1200 kg slowing from 20 m/s to rest has a change in momentum of 1200 × 20 = 24 000 kg m/s.

Force equals the change in momentum divided by the time taken for that change. Force, F, in newtons, N; m ∆v is the change in momentum in kg m/s; ∆t is the time in seconds, s. This equation is provided on the AQA Physics equation sheet, so it does not have to be recalled, but it does have to be selected and used correctly.

concepts.term: Force as the rate of change of momentum
concepts.def: 'Rate of change of momentum' means the change in momentum divided by the time taken, not the total momentum divided by the time. Force equals that rate: for one fixed change in momentum, the longer the change takes, the smaller the force.

concepts.term: Combining F = m × a with a = (v − u)/t
concepts.def: Substituting the acceleration equation into the force equation gives F = m(v − u)/t. Since (v − u) is the change in velocity, ∆v, and t is the time for that change, ∆t, this is F = (m ∆v)/(∆t). The momentum equation is not a new law — it is Newton's Second Law written in terms of momentum.

concepts.term: Increasing the time of a collision
concepts.def: In a crash or a landing, the change in momentum is fixed by how fast the person was going and by their mass — it cannot be reduced by the safety feature. What the safety feature changes is ∆t. Increasing the time taken for the momentum to fall to zero reduces m ∆v ÷ ∆t, and so reduces the force on the person.

Air bags, seat belts, gymnasium crash mats, cycle helmets and cushioned surfaces for playgrounds all work the same way: they deform, stretch or squash, so the person is brought to rest over a longer time. The rate of change of momentum is smaller, so the force on the person is smaller.

Force, mass, velocity and acceleration are linked through F = m a, a = (v − u)/t and F = (m ∆v)/(∆t). Holding the change in momentum fixed and making the time five times longer makes the force five times smaller; holding the time fixed and doubling the change in velocity doubles the force. Explaining a safety feature means saying which quantity is held fixed and which one has been changed.

mcqs.q: The specification defines momentum by an equation. Which word equation is that definition?
options: momentum = mass × acceleration
momentum = weight × velocity
momentum = force × velocity
momentum = mass × velocity
mcqs.explain: This is the defining equation given in 4.5.7.1, and it is one of the equations students are required to recall.

mcqs.q: The momentum equation is written in symbols as p = m v. What do p, m and v stand for?
options: power, mass and velocity
pressure, mass and velocity
momentum, mass and velocity
momentum, mass and volume
mcqs.explain: The specification states momentum, p; mass, m; velocity, v, and these are the only meanings that give the unit kg m/s.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the unit of momentum given in the specification?
options: the newton, N, the same unit as force
the joule, J, the same unit as energy
the kilograms metre per second, kg m/s
the metre per second, m/s, as for speed
mcqs.explain: The unit follows from the equation: kilograms multiplied by metres per second gives kg m/s, exactly as the specification states.

mcqs.q: A ball of mass 250 g is travelling at 6 m/s. What is its momentum?
options: 1500 kg m/s
0.75 kg m/s
1.5 kg m/s
0.042 kg m/s
mcqs.explain: 250 g is 0.25 kg, and 0.25 × 6 = 1.5 kg m/s, with the mass in kilograms as the specification requires.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the units used in p = m v is correct?
options: The velocity must be in m/s and the mass in kg.
The velocity must be in km/h and the mass in kg.
The velocity must be in m/s and the mass in g.
The velocity must be in m/s and the mass in N.
mcqs.explain: The specification gives mass, m, in kilograms, kg and velocity, v, in metres per second, m/s, which together give momentum in kg m/s.

mcqs.q: A sprinter of mass 60 kg is running at 8 m/s. What is the sprinter's momentum?
options: 240 kg m/s
480 kg m/s
3840 kg m/s
7.5 kg m/s
mcqs.explain: p = m v = 60 × 8 = 480 kg m/s, with both quantities already in SI units.

mcqs.q: A lorry of mass 8000 kg is moving at 2 m/s. A car of mass 1000 kg is moving at 20 m/s. Which has the greater momentum?
options: The lorry, because its mass is eight times larger.
The car, because 1000 × 20 gives 20 000 kg m/s.
They are equal, as the mass and speed compensate.
The car, because it is travelling ten times faster.
mcqs.explain: The car's 20 000 kg m/s beats the lorry's 8000 × 2 = 16 000 kg m/s: both quantities have to be multiplied.

mcqs.q: A van of mass 900 kg has a momentum of 3600 kg m/s. What is its velocity?
options: 8 m/s
4 m/s
mcqs.explain: Rearranging p = m v gives v = p / m = 3600 ÷ 900 = 4 m/s, and kg m/s ÷ kg leaves m/s.

mcqs.q: A student works out the momentum of a trolley and writes the answer as '12 N'. What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing is wrong; momentum is a force, so newtons are right.
The unit should be kg m/s, since momentum is mass × velocity.
The unit should be joules, since momentum is a form of energy.
The unit should be m/s, because momentum measures how fast it goes.
mcqs.explain: Multiplying kilograms by metres per second gives kilograms metre per second, the unit the specification states for momentum.

mcqs.q: Which of these completes the specification's statement of conservation of momentum correctly?
options: In a closed system, the total momentum before an event is greater than the total after it.
In a closed system, the total momentum before an event is shared equally after it.
In a closed system, the total momentum before an event is equal to the total after it.
In any system at all, the total momentum before an event is equal to the total after it.
mcqs.explain: This is the statement given in 4.5.7.2, with both the closed-system condition and the equality intact.

mcqs.q: What name does the specification give to the rule that the total momentum of a closed system is the same before and after an event?
options: the conservation of momentum
Newton's Second Law of motion
the principle of moments
the conservation of energy
mcqs.explain: The specification states directly: this is called conservation of momentum.

mcqs.q: Trolley A has a mass of 2 kg and moves at 3 m/s towards a stationary 1 kg trolley B. The two trolleys form a closed system. What is their total momentum immediately after the collision?
options: 9 kg m/s
3 kg m/s
0 kg m/s
6 kg m/s
mcqs.explain: Before the event the total is 2 × 3 = 6 kg m/s, and in a closed system the total afterwards is equal to it.

mcqs.q: A moving snooker ball strikes a stationary ball of equal mass head-on and stops dead. Which description of this event is correct?
options: All the momentum has been transferred to the second ball.
The momentum of the first ball has simply disappeared.
Both balls now share the momentum equally between them.
The second ball gains twice the momentum the first had.
mcqs.explain: The total must be unchanged, so the momentum the first ball lost is now carried by the second, which has the same mass and so the same speed.

mcqs.q: A 2 kg trolley moving at 3 m/s collides with a stationary 1 kg trolley, and the two move off joined together. What is their velocity after the collision?
options: 3 m/s
6 m/s
2 m/s
mcqs.explain: Momentum before is 2 × 3 = 6 kg m/s; after the collision the moving mass is 3 kg, so 6 ÷ 3 = 2 m/s.

mcqs.q: A 0.5 kg ball moving to the right at 4 m/s meets a 0.3 kg ball moving to the left at 2 m/s. Taking right as the positive direction, what is the total momentum of the two balls before they collide?
options: 2.6 kg m/s to the right
0.8 kg m/s to the right
1.4 kg m/s to the right
1.4 kg m/s to the left
mcqs.explain: The momenta are +2.0 kg m/s and −0.6 kg m/s, and 2.0 − 0.6 = 1.4 kg m/s in the positive, rightward direction.

mcqs.q: Two skaters stand at rest on ice and push each other apart. One has a mass of 60 kg and moves off at 1.5 m/s. The other has a mass of 45 kg. What is her velocity?
options: 90 m/s
2 m/s
mcqs.explain: Total momentum before is zero, so 60 × 1.5 = 45 × v, giving v = 2 m/s in the opposite direction.

mcqs.q: The specification states what happens when a force acts on an object that is moving, or able to move. What occurs?
options: a change in the momentum of the object
a change in the weight of the object
an increase in momentum, never a decrease
no change of momentum until it stops
mcqs.explain: This is the statement in 4.5.7.3, and it holds whether the momentum increases or decreases.

mcqs.q: Which two equations does the specification combine to give F = (m ∆v)/(∆t)?
options: F = m × a and a = (v − u)/t
E = ½ m v² and a = (v − u)/t
W = F s and a = (v − u)/t
p = m v and a = (v − u)/t
mcqs.explain: Substituting a = (v − u)/t into F = m × a gives F = m(v − u)/t, which is F = (m ∆v)/(∆t).

mcqs.q: A car of mass 1200 kg travelling at 20 m/s is brought to rest in 0.10 s when it hits a wall. Using F = (m ∆v)/(∆t), which is given on the equation sheet, what is the average force on the car?
In the equation F = (m ∆v)/(∆t), what does the quantity m ∆v represent?
options: the total momentum of the object
the change in momentum of the object
the mass times the final velocity
the force acting on the object
mcqs.explain: The specification states that m ∆v = change in momentum, and its unit is kg m/s, not newtons.

mcqs.q: The specification says that force equals the rate of change of momentum. What does 'rate of change of momentum' mean?
options: the change in momentum divided by the time taken
the total momentum divided by the time taken
the change in momentum multiplied by the time
the momentum an object has at a given moment
mcqs.explain: 'Rate of' means divided by time and 'change of momentum' means m ∆v, which together give F = (m ∆v)/(∆t).

mcqs.q: A car is fitted with an air bag, which inflates in front of the driver during a crash. Why does the air bag reduce the force on the driver?
options: It makes the change in the driver's momentum much smaller.
It makes the driver's momentum change over a longer time.
It brings the driver to a stop far more quickly and safely.
It soaks up the force of the crash inside the bag of gas.
mcqs.explain: The bag increases ∆t while m ∆v stays the same, so the rate of change of momentum, and therefore the force, is smaller.

mcqs.q: A gymnast lands on a thick crash mat rather than on the bare floor. Which explanation of the mat's effect is correct?
options: The mat reduces the gymnast's momentum on landing.
The mat stops the gymnast in a much shorter time.
The mat absorbs the force before it reaches the gymnast.
The mat increases the stopping time, so the force is less.
mcqs.explain: The mat squashes, so the same change in momentum happens over a longer ∆t and F = (m ∆v)/(∆t) is smaller.

mcqs.q: Two identical cars, each of mass 1200 kg, hit a wall at 20 m/s. Car A stops in 0.10 s. Car B has a crumple zone and stops in 0.50 s. Which statement is correct?
options: Car B's change in momentum is five times smaller than car A's.
The force on car B is the same, because the cars are identical.
The force on car B is five times greater than the force on car A.
The force on car B is one fifth of the force on car A.
mcqs.explain: The same 24 000 kg m/s spread over five times the time gives one fifth of the force: 48 000 N instead of 240 000 N.

mcqs.q: A lorry of mass 12 000 kg is parked at the side of the road. What is its momentum?
options: 12 000 kg m/s, from its mass alone
zero, since its velocity is zero
very large, because its mass is large
impossible to say without its weight
mcqs.explain: p = m v, and any mass multiplied by a velocity of zero gives a momentum of zero.
